claims.text: Conventional boride-based alloys used in hot-dip aluminum plating exhibit moderate resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Chromium doping will cause a stable Cr-rich oxide layer to form on the boride-based alloy.
The Cr-rich oxide layer will be dense and adherent.
Chromium preferentially oxidizes at high temperature.
The resulting Cr-rich oxide acts as a protective barrier against molten aluminum.
The protective oxide barrier limits aluminum penetration into the boride-based alloy.
The protective oxide barrier reduces dissolution of the boride material.
Chromium doping will significantly reduce molten-aluminum corrosion relative to an undoped boride-based alloy.
Chromium-doped samples will have lower mass loss than undoped samples after molten-aluminum exposure.
Chromium-doped samples will show less surface degradation than undoped samples after molten-aluminum exposure.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating temperatures are approximately 660–750 °C.
The protective effect may diminish at temperatures above the stated typical plating range.
The protective effect may diminish under conditions that inhibit stable oxide formation.

contradictions.description: The uncertainty field states that the optimal chromium concentration still requires validation, while the experimental design presupposes inclusion of an 'optimized amount' without defining how that amount is established.
